items.t: JSE: CFR Share Price Holds the Uptrend Despite Dip, as Swiss Luxury Group Richemont Posts Strong First Half Results
sum: Richemont delivered stronger-than-expected first-half profits, but slowing growth at jewelry houses triggered an early sell-off, with the JSE-listed shares finding support again at the 100-week moving average.
- Richemont reported stronger-than-expected first-half profits, with operating profit increasing 38% to €3.13 billion.
- Concerns about slowing growth in its jewelry division led to an early sell-off of shares, despite overall strong performance.
- The jewelry houses, including Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, saw revenue growth slow to 14% in the second quarter, missing analyst expectations.
- Richemont's share price found support at the 100-week moving average, indicating a potential for maintaining its long-term bullish trend.

Richemont (JSE: CFR) shares came under pressure at Friday’s open after the luxury group reported first-half results that comfortably exceeded analyst expectations. However, concerns about slowing growth in its jewelry division, its most important business, triggered profit-taking before the stock recovered most of its early losses.

The jewelry houses, including Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Buccellati and Vhernier, remain the group’s primary growth engine. However, quarterly revenue growth slowed to 14% at constant exchange rates in the second quarter, compared with 24% in the first quarter. The latest figure also missed analyst expectations of 16%.

sum: В пятницу, 13 ноября 2026 года, Richemont сообщила о сильных результатах за первое полугодие за шесть месяцев, закончившихся 30 сентября. В своем заявлении Richemont, опубликованном GlobeNewswire, швейцарская группа компаний класса люкс сообщила, что объем продаж достиг 12,3 млрд евро, что на 16 процентов выше по фактическому обменному курсу и на 17 процентов по постоянному курсу.

Рост оставался широким, несмотря на нестабильный геополитический и макроэкономический фон. Продажи во втором квартале увеличились на 13 процентов при неизменных темпах после 20-процентного роста в первом квартале и 14-процентного роста в предыдущем году.

Ювелирные дома, в том числе Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Buccellati и Vhernier, увеличили продажи в первом полугодии на 18 процентов по фактическому обменному курсу и на 19 процентов по постоянному курсу. Операционный результат сегмента составил 3,2 миллиарда евро по сравнению с 2,5 миллиарда евро годом ранее. Операционная рентабельность составила 35,3 процента, или 33,4 процента без учета положительных разовых статей.

Richemont отметил, что спрос на культовые коллекции ювелирных изделий и часов остается высоким во всех регионах. Группа придерживалась взвешенного подхода к ценообразованию, продолжая инвестировать в свою розничную сеть и производственные мощности, даже несмотря на то, что затраты на сырье оставались высокими.

Специализированные часовщики увеличили продажи на 9 процентов по фактическому обменному курсу и на 10 процентов по постоянному курсу, до 1,7 миллиарда евро. Во втором квартале рост ускорился до 12 процентов при неизменных темпах. Подразделение возглавляли Vacheron Constantin, Jaeger-LeCoultre и A. Lange & Söhne, поддерживаемые признанными коллекциями и новыми продуктами.

Операционная прибыль подразделения выросла до 150 миллионов евро с 50 миллионов евро в предыдущем году. Операционная рентабельность достигла 8,8 процента, или 7,7 процента без учета положительных разовых статей. Richemont предупредил, что восстановление может не быть линейным, поскольку спрос в Китае все еще вялый, а ситуация в отрасли сложная.

Япония, Америка и Азиатско-Тихоокеанский регион лидировали по региональным показателям, в то время как Европа также продемонстрировала рост. Ближний Восток и Африка были единственным регионом, в котором не наблюдался рост, что отражало более слабый спрос на фоне продолжающегося конфликта. Продажи напрямую клиентам составили 78 процентов продаж группы, что на два процентных пункта больше, чем в предыдущем году.

sum: South African billionaire Johann Rupert's Compagnie Financière Richemont SA is expected to lean on its jewelry brands again when it reports results for the six months to Sept. 30 on Friday, Nov. 13.

The Geneva-based owner of Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels is set to benefit from continued demand for high-end jewelry, which has carried the group through a slowdown that has hit much of the luxury industry. Its watch business has grown at a slower pace.

The first quarter showed the gap. Sales rose 20% at constant exchange rates to €6.3 billion ($7.1 billion) in the three months to June 30. Sales at the Jewellery Maisons division, which includes Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels and Buccellati, climbed 24%, while the specialist watchmakers, a group that includes IWC Schaffhausen, Jaeger-LeCoultre and Panerai, posted an 8% increase.
Richemont's own stores did most of the work. Sales through directly operated boutiques rose 24% and made up 71% of the group's revenue in the quarter, while online sales grew 18%.

Investors will also look for any comment on De Beers. Botswana has backed a consortium seeking to buy Anglo American Plc's stake in the diamond producer, and Richemont's name has come up in the discussion. The company has not confirmed that it is taking part.
A move into diamond mining would be a departure for a group built on luxury brands and retail.

Rupert, 76, is chairman of Richemont and the group's controlling shareholder. His holding company, Compagnie Financière Rupert, owns all of Richemont's B shares, which give him about 51% of the voting rights while representing about 9% of the company's economic value. Richemont's A shares trade in Zurich, with a secondary listing in Johannesburg.

items.t: Richemont stock weighs De Beers role after Botswana backs bid
sum: Richemont is weighing a possible role in the Global Diamond Consortium after Botswana backed the group as its preferred bidder for Anglo American's stake in De Beers. The development was reported by Reuters on November 9, 2026.

Since the latest relevant in-house report on November 9, Richemont stock has moved from 185.48 euros at 5:01 p.m. Berlin time to 190.75 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 5:53 p.m. CET on Wednesday, November 11, a gain of 2.84 percent. This comparison is against the earlier in-house quote, not an Xetra closing price.

Botswana President Duma Boko said the country's De Beers holding would rise from 15 percent to 30 percent if the proposed transaction is completed. Botswana would then become De Beers' largest individual shareholder and has backed the consortium led by former De Beers chief executive Gareth Penny.

Anglo American is seeking to sell its 85 percent interest in De Beers. Reuters reported that Namibia and Angola would participate in the transaction, while Penny said the consortium was also working with Oman toward a co-ownership structure. Anglo American said binding transaction documents still had to be agreed.

Richemont is among the companies discussing a role in the consortium, alongside jewellery businesses and diamond industry participants. The group owns Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, giving a possible De Beers investment a direct link to its natural-diamond supply chain.

Richemont has not confirmed participation, and no investment size or final terms have been disclosed. Investors therefore cannot yet assess the potential earnings impact, capital commitment or exposure to De Beers' pressured diamond market.

Richemont is scheduled to publish its fiscal first-half results on Friday, November 13. Investors will focus on jewellery demand, regional performance, margins and any update on the De Beers discussions.

sum: Richemont is facing a new strategic decision in the De Beers sale after Botswana selected the Global Diamond Consortium as its preferred bidder for Anglo American's interest in the diamond producer on Monday, November 9. Reuters reported that Botswana plans to increase its De Beers stake to 30 percent from 15 percent.

The Reuters report said Botswana will become De Beers' largest single shareholder and that Namibia and Angola will also take part in the transaction. Anglo American is selling an 85 percent interest in the diamond producer.

The development adds weight to earlier reports that Richemont is discussing membership in the Global Diamond Consortium, led by former De Beers chief executive Gareth Penny. The Edge Malaysia, carrying a Reuters report, said the possible transaction could give Richemont greater influence over a key part of its natural-diamond supply chain.

Richemont has not confirmed that it will join the consortium. No participation terms or investment size have been disclosed, so the financial effect for the luxury group cannot yet be assessed. The proposal also carries exposure to a diamond market pressured by weaker prices and competition from laboratory-grown stones.

Richemont owns Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, linking a potential De Beers role to its established jewellery businesses. The company last reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 sales growth of 20 percent at constant exchange rates, while its fiscal first-half results are scheduled for Friday, November 13.

items.t: Richemont stock weighs strategic role in De Beers consortium
sum: Richemont is weighing whether to join the Global Diamond Consortium in a bid for De Beers, according to a report published by Merca2 on Friday, November 6. The report said negotiations involving Richemont and Signet Jewelers were advanced, while the proposed transaction remains a strategic discussion rather than a completed acquisition.

The real-time quote of Richemont stock was 183.43 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:08 CET on Friday, November 6. The possible consortium role puts Richemont's position in the natural-diamond supply chain at the center of investor attention, but the report did not establish a final commitment or transaction terms.

Merca2 said analysts see jewelry as more resilient than other luxury categories, particularly leather goods. Jefferies expects group growth to moderate as the comparison base becomes tougher, while margin leverage could improve as input-cost and foreign-exchange pressures ease.

The report cited Jefferies' expectation of 13.1 percent organic group growth in the second quarter before currency effects. Jewelry was expected to advance 17 percent, with first-half operating profit forecast to rise 20 percent year over year to 2.839 billion euros. These are analyst expectations, not Richemont's reported results.

Citi was reported to have raised its price target to 227 Swiss francs from 224 Swiss francs and retained a Buy recommendation. RBC Capital Markets viewed a possible Richemont investment in the consortium as strategically relevant for the long-term positioning of natural diamonds, but not as a material near-term financial event.

Richemont's jewelry maisons include Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels and Buccellati. Merca2 said their resilience and product expansion could help the group gain share in jewelry, which represents about 55 percent of group revenue according to the report.

The main risk is that support for the natural-diamond ecosystem becomes a sustained capital commitment. De Beers posted a loss of 511 million US dollars in fiscal 2025, and the report pointed to possible additional spending on the Jwaneng mine and on efforts to strengthen demand for natural diamonds.

SMI Holds Above 15,000 at Midday as Oil Relief Supports Swiss Shares
sum: The SMI remained above the 15,000-point threshold in Thursday midday trading, but the Swiss blue-chip index had surrendered most of its early advance. At 12:27:51 Berlin time on November 5, 2026, the index stood at 15,034.32 points, up 0.08 percent from the previous session's close of 15,022.85 points, according to finanzen.ch.

The SMI opened at 15,061.17 points, equivalent to a 0.255 percent gain against Wednesday's close. It subsequently reached an intraday high of 15,092.56 points before retreating toward the 15,000-point mark. The midday reading therefore represented only a modest increase from the prior close and was not a closing value.

Trading remained volatile among individual index constituents. Holcim, Sika, Lonza, Swiss Re and Richemont were among the stronger shares listed in the midday market report, while Alcon, Logitech, ABB, Novartis and Nestle were among the weaker performers. The source reported the SMI's intraday low at 14,995.55 points.

The broader market backdrop remained supportive after the sharp fall in oil prices on Wednesday. Lower energy costs reduced immediate concerns about inflation and future interest-rate pressure, helping risk assets extend the previous session's gains. The relief was also linked in market coverage to hopes that political developments in the United States could contribute to a de-escalation of the conflict involving Iran.

That support was not uniform. The market continued to weigh geopolitical risks, inflation and interest-rate expectations, while selected technology and growth-sensitive shares faced pressure. For investors, the midday picture was therefore one of consolidation above 15,000 rather than a broad-based acceleration. items.t: SIG vs. CFRUY: Which Stock Is the Better Value Option?
sum: Investors interested in Retail - Jewelry stocks are likely familiar with Signet (SIG) and Compagnie Financiere Richemont AG (CFRUY). But which of these two companies is the best option for those looking for undervalued stocks? Let's take a closer look.

Everyone has their own methods for finding great value opportunities, but our model includes pairing an impressive grade in the Value category of our Style Scores system with a strong Zacks Rank. The Zacks Rank favors stocks with strong earnings estimate revision trends, and our Style Scores highlight companies with specific traits.

Currently, Signet has a Zacks Rank of #1 (Strong Buy), while Compagnie Financiere Richemont AG has a Zacks Rank of #4 (Sell). The Zacks Rank favors stocks that have recently seen positive revisions to their earnings estimates, so investors should rest assured that SIG has an improving earnings outlook. But this is just one piece of the puzzle for value investors.
Value investors also try to analyze a wide range of traditional figures and metrics to help determine whether a company is undervalued at its current share price levels.

The Style Score Value grade factors in a variety of key fundamental metrics, including the popular P/E ratio, P/S ratio, earnings yield, cash flow per share, and a number of other key stats that are commonly used by value investors.

SIG currently has a forward P/E ratio of 10.05, while CFRUY has a forward P/E of 24.04. We also note that SIG has a PEG ratio of 0.65. This popular metric is similar to the widely-known P/E ratio, with the difference being that the PEG ratio also takes into account the company's expected earnings growth rate. CFRUY currently has a PEG ratio of 1.44.

Another notable valuation metric for SIG is its P/B ratio of 2.48. Investors use the P/B ratio to look at a stock's market value versus its book value, which is defined as total assets minus total liabilities. By comparison, CFRUY has a P/B of 7.71.

sum: - Johann Rupert has appointed his son, Anton Rupert, as non-executive co-deputy chairman of luxury group Richemont, signalling succession plans.
- Anton will be responsible for Richemont’s creative and commercial strategy, joining Bram Schot, who oversees corporate governance.
- The Rupert family maintains control over Richemont, owning about 10% of equity but holding over half of the voting rights.
- Richemont has outperformed some competitors amid a tough luxury market, aided by strong jewellery sales and portfolio adjustments.

The 76-year-old chairman has appointed his 39-year-old son, Anton Rupert, as non-executive co-deputy chairman, putting him in charge of the group’s creative and commercial direction. Anton has been on Richemont’s board since 2017.

The move gives investors their clearest signal yet that succession planning is underway at the Swiss luxury group, which owns some of the world’s best-known jewellery and watch brands, including Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels.

Investors have been asking for more clarity on the issue since Richemont reshuffled its senior management in 2024, per Bloomberg's report. Rupert controls the company through a family trust, owning about 10% of its equity but more than half of its voting rights.

sum: Cartier has opened its first New Zealand boutique, on Auckland's Queen Street, extending the reach of the jewellery house that has driven most of the recent gains in South African billionaire Johann Rupert's fortune.
The store at 66 Queen St opened quietly on 31 July and launched officially on Wednesday. It is Cartier's eighth in Oceania and takes the brand past 270 stores worldwide.

Rupert controls Compagnie Financière Richemont, the Swiss group that owns Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Montblanc and Chloé. He holds 10.18 percent of the equity but 51 percent of the voting rights, through a dual-class structure of 6.26 million A shares and 522 million B shares a stake that gives him unchallenged control of a company that recently crossed CHF100 billion in market value.

Jewellery is what is working. Richemont's jewellery houses, led by Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, lifted sales 14 percent to €16.5 billion ($17.8 billion) against group revenue of €22.4 billion ($24.2 billion), up 11 percent at constant currencies. The group overtook Walmart this year to become the second-largest watch and jewellery seller in North America, on $3.62 billion of sales.
Forbes valued Rupert at about $17.4 billion in August, after a run attributed largely to record Cartier and Van Cleef sales.

Richemont now has Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels and Montblanc trading within the same stretch of Queen Street an unusually dense cluster for a market of five million people, and a sign the group sees Auckland as underserved rather than saturated.
The boutique's design nods to Cartier's Parisian origins while housing New Zealand work, including a hand-carved tōtara piece by Māori carver Steve Solomon and hand-blown glass by Isaac Katzoff.

items.t: Global Personal Luxury Goods Market to Reach $737.38 Billion by 2030 as Digital Commerce and Affluent Consumer Demand Accelerate - Featuring Profiles of LVMH, Kering and Richemont Among Other Key Players
sum: Opportunities center on affluent Asian demand, AI personalization, sustainable materials, digital and metaverse retail, experiential formats, limited editions, resale and influencer-led branding
Dublin, Sept. 02, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The "Personal Luxury Goods Market Report 2026" has been added to ResearchAndMarkets.com's offering.

The global personal luxury goods market is experiencing rapid expansion, supported by rising discretionary spending, strong brand loyalty and growing demand for premium, exclusive products. The market is projected to increase from $428.24 billion in 2025 to $476.6 billion in 2026, representing a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 11.3%. Historical growth has been supported by the dominance of heritage brands, craftsmanship-led product differentiation, traditional in-store purchasing behavior and sustained demand among affluent consumers.

Looking ahead, the personal luxury goods market is forecast to reach $737.38 billion by 2030, expanding at a CAGR of 11.5%. Key growth drivers include artificial intelligence-powered personalization in luxury retail, the continued expansion of digital luxury marketplaces and increasing demand for sustainable materials. Luxury brands are also broadening their presence in emerging economies, where rising incomes and changing consumer preferences are creating new opportunities for premium fashion, accessories, watches, jewelry and beauty products.

Several personal luxury goods market trends are expected to shape the industry through 2030. These include the rise of experiential luxury retail, stronger demand for limited-edition and personalized products, and the expansion of resale platforms and circular luxury business models. Celebrity partnerships, influencer-led campaigns and digital-first commerce platforms are also playing a larger role in purchasing decisions. In addition, metaverse-based experiences and other immersive digital channels are enabling brands to engage consumers beyond conventional retail environments.

The expanding high-net-worth population remains a significant driver of market growth. Greater wealth accumulation, supported by financial market performance and economic expansion, is increasing purchasing power for premium products.

sum: Richemont sales expanded nearly twice as strongly as expected in the quarter through the end of June, supported by robust demand among wealthy Americans for its Cartier rings and bracelets.
Sales rose by 20% at constant exchange rates, the Swiss luxury group said Wednesday, almost double the Bloomberg consensus forecast for quarterly expansion of 11%.

The jewellery division, which accounts for about three-quarters of Richemont's business, posted growth of 24%, with sales in the Americas region jumping 27%, and the specialist watchmakers segment expanded by 8%. Overall sales advanced across all regions, including a return to growth in the Middle East and Africa, where Richemont gets just under a 10th of its revenue.

The positive report is further evidence that the Geneva-based company has coped better with the broader slowdown in the luxury sector than rivals like LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE, Gucci-owner Kering SA and Hermes International SCA, helped by the enduring appeal of brands including Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels.

In times of economic uncertainty, high-end jewellery is seen as a superior store of value than expensive apparel and leather goods. Shares in Geneva-based Richemont have risen by about 6% this year through Tuesday's close and are up by nearly a quarter over the past 12 months.
Richemont has also noted that envy of success is less widespread among Americans than Europeans, which helps underpin luxury spending in the US market.

In recent months, the high-end sector has been struggling with a collapse in demand from China, as well as higher gold prices and fallout from the conflict in the Middle East, which disrupted travel in the region and hurt sales at duty-free shopping hubs like Dubai.

items.t: European Luxury Stocks Surge on Proposed US-Iran Peace Deal
sum: Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.

European luxury equities experienced a massive valuation surge on Friday, June 12, following the publication of a proposed 14-point peace memorandum between the U.S. and Iran. The tentative diplomatic framework, which outlines the lifting of U.S. oil sanctions and the guaranteed reopening of the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, triggered an immediate risk-on rotation across continental trading floors.

Shares in high-end design houses LVMH, Kering, and Hermès skyrocketed by roughly 5%, leading a broader market rally that pushed the pan-European STOXX 600 index up 1.8% to reverse weeks of energy-driven stagflation fears.

The explosive rebound across luxury portfolios followed an official report from Iranian state media detailing a comprehensive diplomatic breakthrough with Washington. According to the leaked memorandum of understanding, Tehran has committed to fully restoring international shipping access through the narrow Strait of Hormuz within 30 days. In exchange, the U.S. will unwind its restrictive crude oil embargoes.

The economic relief was immediate. Prior to the announcement, the effective closure of the primary maritime channel had sent energy prices surging, fueling persistent inflation fears that forced the European Central Bank to implement hawkish interest-rate adjustments. While President Donald Trump later tempered the market enthusiasm via social media by stating that the accord was subject to the finalization of official documents, reports confirm that senior diplomats are on track to sign the treaty ahead of the upcoming Group of Seven leaders' summit.

The luxury sector emerged as the primary beneficiary of this geopolitical de-escalation. In Paris, LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE and Gucci owner Kering SA both jumped 5%, while ultra-premium leather goods titan Hermès International advanced nearly 5%. In Zurich, Cartier parent Richemont rose 3.4%.

GCQ’s Tynan bets big on luxury stocks amid AI chip ‘bubble’
sum: Earlier this year, GCQ’s high-profile investment chief Doug Tynan rapidly sold down his shares in luxury goods companies Louis Vuitton, Richemont and Hermes to fund a $200 million bet on software stocks, which had been sold off from fears that artificial intelligence would destroy their businesses.

At the time, luxury stocks had been on a tear from an investor flight to safety as the so-called SaaSpocalypse pervaded global markets. But the sector has more recently been battered by the Iran war as the skyrocketing oil price hits consumer spending.

items.t: 4 Takeaways From Luxury’s Q1 Earnings
sum: Luxury’s hopes for a slight first-quarter rebound have been set back, as conflict in the Middle East delivers a blow to performance.

“Q1 didn’t really change the sector’s outlook, and, if anything, it slowed down or pushed back the recovery story we had in mind,” Barclays head of European luxury goods research Carole Madjo says. “The market has lowered its Q2 estimates to factor in the impact of the Middle East conflict and the disrupted tourism environment. The sector’s downgrade cycle is still ongoing on the top line, and potentially on margins as well.”
HSBC anticipated a 5.5% increase in global luxury sales in Q1 2026. However, the average organic sales growth of LVMH, Kering, Hermès, Moncler, and Prada materialized at 4.2%.

“For most companies, momentum in China is improving every quarter. The big issue continues to be the drop in Chinese tourism,” TD Cowen analyst Oliver Chen says. “The US continues to be a resilient and attractive market, with a K-shaped economy — where the top end grows, but the lower end is seeing more pressure particularly as consumers watch gas prices. The strongest momentum comes from jewelry.”

While soft luxury brands have shown relative weakness, the jewelry “supercycle” continues. Sales at LVMH’s watches and jewelry division, Kering’s jewelry arm, and Hermès jewelry were up 7%, 22%, and almost 10%, respectively. This bodes well for Cartier owner Richemont, which will publish its annual earnings on May 22.

At LVMH’s annual general meeting on April 23, chair and CEO Bernard Arnault warned investors that the Middle East crisis “could turn into a global catastrophe with extremely serious and very negative economic consequences”. He added: “In which case, who can say how 2026 will play out? Or it might be resolved one way or another more quickly, which is what we all hope for, even if it doesn’t seem easy; and in that case, business will gradually return to normal.”
Despite variation between companies, the conflict in the Middle East has impacted sales growth by around 1 to 2 percentage points.

items.t: Another South African billionaire moves to divest - this time for $29 billion
sum: - South African billionaire Nathan Kirsh is seeking to sell Restaurant Depot LLC for about $29 billion, with Sysco Corp. nearing a deal.
- Kirsh pioneered the cash-and-carry business model in the U.S., enabling small restaurant owners to buy supplies at any time from warehouses.
- Restaurant Depot, founded in 1976 as Jetro Cash & Carry, now controls a major share of the U.S. restaurant supply market with 166 locations in 35 states.
- Both Jetro and Restaurant Depot operate under Jetro Holdings, forming a nationwide warehouse network focused on supporting small food businesses.

Much like fellow South African billionaire Johann Rupert, who divested from Swiss watchmaker Baume & Mercier earlier this year, Nathan Kirsh is currently seeking to sell Restaurant Depot LLC, one of his most significant assets, for an estimated $29 billion.
At the center of this deal is Sysco Corp., a large U.S. food distributor, which is close to sealing the deal, as seen in a report by the Wall Street Journal.

After pioneering what is now known as the cash-and-carry business model, which lets small-restaurant owners and other independent businesses pick up food supplies from any of his warehouses at any time, the South African billionaire founded Restaurant Depot.

Middle East conflict hits luxury brands as wealthy Gulf consumers pull back
sum: Millions of Muslims worldwide are marking Eid al-Fitr this Thursday and through the weekend, ending the month of Ramadan. But across the Middle East, the usual celebrations, family vacations and holiday shopping have largely been scaled back since the war began.

In Israel, malls have reported a recent uptick in visitor spending, including what retailers describe as “emotional purchases” between missile barrages. In contrast, the luxury market in the UAE and across the Persian Gulf has slowed sharply.

This is no marginal market. Consumers in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait account for about 10% of global luxury purchasing power, a significant blow to fashion houses already facing economic headwinds. Who would be inclined to buy a $10,000 Chanel bag when there's war outside?

According to Reuters, Chalhoub Group, which operates about 900 stores for brands including Versace, Jimmy Choo and Sephora across the region, said its Bahrain locations have closed. Stores elsewhere, including in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Jordan, remain open, but staff attendance is voluntary.

Amazon has shut down operations at its Abu Dhabi distribution centers, suspended regional deliveries and instructed employees in Saudi Arabia and Jordan to stay home. Kering, which owns Gucci, Balenciaga and Saint Laurent, temporarily closed stores in the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar and suspended travel to the Middle East.

Despite drones flying over Dubai and Abu Dhabi, authorities in the UAE have sought to project "business as usual". On March 2, shortly after the war began, a video circulated showing UAE President and ruler of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, walking through Dubai Mall, one of the largest shopping centers in the world, in what appeared to be an effort to signal stability.

Dubai Mall spans about 1.1 million square meters, with about half dedicated to retail. It houses more than 1,200 stores, including dozens of flagship luxurious boutiques for brands such as Chanel, Gucci, Dior and Louis Vuitton. Annual sales run into the billions of dollars, with international tourism playing a key role, particularly in luxury fashion.

Luxury stocks slump as Middle East conflict risks one of the sector’s 'few bright spots’
sum: Luxury stocks were among the hardest hit sectors early Tuesday, with European markets heading for another day of losses as the conflict in the Middle East intensified overnight.

Shares of conglomerate LVMH, Gucci-owner Kering, and British outerwear maker Burberry were among the worst performers, with week-to-date losses approaching 10% each. The wider European blue-chip index, Stoxx 600, was down nearly 3% Tuesday, after falling 1.6% on Monday.
The Middle East has been a driver of growth in the sector, which is battling a difficult macroeconomic backdrop, and many formerly best-selling brands are struggling to resonate with consumers.
The region's strength, however, hasn't been enough to offset weakness elsewhere, notably in China, and industry giants like LVMH and Kering are still struggling to get sales back on a positive track.

"The Middle East has been one of the few bright spots," Morningstar analyst Jelena Sokolova told CNBC. "You have one area which was small, but which was very, very vibrant, and it's being affected now."

The U.S. and Israel launched widespread attacks on Iran over the weekend that killed the country's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Iran responded with retaliatory strikes, and the conflict now engulfs the wider Middle East region with no clear endpoint in sight.
U.S. President Donald Trump has said the war could last for four to five weeks, but that it could go on "far longer than that."

Cartier’s Parent Company Saw Its Sales Hit a Record $7.4 Billion in Q3
sum: A slew of holiday shoppers helped Richemont enter 2026 with a bang.

Cartier's parent company saw its sales jump 11 percent in Q3 to about $7.43 billion (€6.4 billion), a new record for the luxe conglomerate, according to a brand report announced today. That figure, bolstered by customers splashing down cash for gifts during the most wonderful time of the year, toppled the 7.5 percent analysts estimated the company would reach, a strong showing even amid Swiss tariff woes and a struggling luxury market, Bloomberg reported.

Hong Kong was a large driver of increased sales for Richemont in Q3, where there was rising demand for the company's goods. The U.S., too, had a strong consumer turnout, increasing sales over the period by a cool 14 percent. Elsewhere, Japan saw a jump of 17 percent, while the Middle East & Africa had an increase of 20 percent during the holiday season.

The brand's jewelry houses were standouts over the time period, seeing a 14 percent increase in sales in the fiscal quarter. Richemont's watch brands, too, snagged a 7 percent boost in Q3; the company is home to names such as Vacheron Constantin, Piaget, and more. That figure, in particular, is impressive, given that the U.S. has placed Swiss exports with a 15 percent tariff (down from a whopping 39 percent earlier in 2025), not to mention gold's sky-high prices. Given the help from luxury shoppers, we may see these struggles take a stronger hold on Richemont's figures in the next quarter, who have already said high material prices and currency and the impact of currency changes may impact growth.

Another piece of the puzzle that may be helping drive customers to Richemont's stores is its celebrity ties, according to Bloomberg. Cartier, for one, counts actors Jacob Elordi and Timothée Chalamet as friends of the house, a.k.a. ambassadors. The former hopped on the Cartier train this past October and has since rocked a Prive Tank Normale with a skeletonized platinum case set with diamonds at the 2026 Golden Globes. As for the latter, he has worked with the brand since 2021; lately, Chalamet has donned a Panthère de Cartier pendant necklace on the Golden Globes red carpet. Even Taylor Swift rocked a Santos Demoiselle when she got engaged to Travis Kelce last year.
